title: North America
lead: The U.S. label rules, then California, Oregon, Washington and New York, plus Canada and its Icewine. This is the Court's Section 8.

intro.title: WHERE THE GRAPES CAME FROM
intro.text: A U.S. place name on a label is an appellation of origin. The smaller the place, the stricter the rule.

sections.name: U.S. wine law and labels

lines.label: The rule book
lines.text: U.S. label rules are federal TTB regulations (27 CFR part 4). An AVA (American Viticultural Area) is a grape-growing region with its own features and a legal boundary, listed in 27 CFR part 9.

lines.label: Grape names
lines.text: A grape name on the front needs at least 75% of that grape. A grape name also needs a place of origin on the label.

know: Variety 75%, AVA 85%, vintage 95% (with an AVA), vineyard name 95%.
With a state or county instead of an AVA, the vintage rule drops to 85%.
'Estate bottled' means the winery grew every grape in the AVA on land it owns or controls, and made and bottled the wine there.
'Reserve' has no legal meaning on a U.S. label.
'Meritage' is a trademark, not a legal grape rule.

visuals.title: How much must match the label
visuals.note: Federal minimums. Oregon is stricter (see Oregon).

items.name: Estate Bottled
items.text: Legal term. Grown, made and bottled by the winery in its AVA.

items.name: Meritage
items.text: A trademark, not a legal category.

sections.name: California · Napa Valley

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Dry Mediterranean. The North Coast is moderate to warm, depending on how close it is to the Pacific or San Pablo Bay.

lines.label: Winemaking
lines.text: Often lots of new French oak, sometimes American, for reds and whites. Chardonnay often goes through malolactic fermentation.

know: Napa was California's first AVA, in 1981.
Napa is only 4% of California's grape harvest.
Carneros is shared by Napa and Sonoma and is cooled by San Pablo Bay. It is known for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine.
Rutherford is Cabernet country; its grainy tannins are called 'Rutherford Dust'.
Producers to know: Opus One, Robert Mondavi, Beringer.

visuals.note: Know which county each AVA sits in.

visuals.title: of California's grape harvest

sections.name: California · Sonoma and Mendocino

lines.label: Where
lines.text: Sonoma, Mendocino and Lake counties sit in the North Coast, north of San Pablo Bay. Physical features to know: the Petaluma Wind Gap and the Mayacamas and Sonoma mountain ranges.

lines.label: Sparkling
lines.text: Cool spots such as Carneros and Mendocino's Anderson Valley make sparkling wine.

know: Russian River Valley: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
Dry Creek Valley: Zinfandel (and Cabernet).
Alexander Valley: Cabernet Sauvignon.
Sonoma Coast is Sonoma County's largest AVA.
Anderson Valley is in Mendocino County, not Sonoma.

visuals.note: Grape notes from Wine Folly; counties from the Court.

sections.name: California · Central Coast

lines.label: Where
lines.text: Coastal counties south of San Francisco Bay and north of the city of Santa Barbara: Monterey, San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara.

lines.label: Wind tunnels
lines.text: Monterey's mountains run northwest to southeast and Santa Barbara's run east to west. Both make cool wind tunnels; Santa Barbara's also brings fog.

know: Monterey and Santa Barbara are cool maritime; closer to the coast is cooler.
Paso Robles (San Luis Obispo County) is warm continental with big day-night swings.
Mountains block Paso Robles from the sea, with only a small gap.
California makes about 81% of U.S. wine.

sections.name: Oregon · Willamette Valley

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Cool Mediterranean with maritime influence. The Coast Range to the west makes a rain shadow; the Cascades are to the east.

know: Pinot Noir is 59% of Oregon's planted acres; Pinot Gris is next at 14%.
David Lett planted the Willamette Valley's first Pinot Noir in 1965 (The Eyrie Vineyards).
Oregon labels need 90% of the named grape (with 18 exceptions) and 95% from the named appellation.
Willamette Valley has two-thirds of Oregon's wineries and vineyards.
Willamette Pinot Noir pairs with salmon.

items.label: OREGON
items.title: Stricter
items.text:
90% named grape
95% from the appellation
100% Oregon grapes

visuals.title: of Oregon's vines are Pinot Noir
visuals.text: Pinot Gris follows at 14% and Chardonnay at 7%.

sections.name: Washington · Columbia Valley

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Warm desert. The Cascades block the rain, so the Columbia Valley gets only 6-8 inches a year and needs irrigation.

lines.label: Soils
lines.text: Loess over gravel and flood sediment on basalt, laid down by the Missoula Floods.

know: Over 99% of Washington's vineyard acreage is in the Columbia Valley.
Washington is the 2nd largest wine producer in the U.S.
The Court's Washington AVAs: Columbia Valley, Yakima Valley, Walla Walla Valley.
Columbia Valley, Walla Walla Valley and Columbia Gorge cross into Oregon.
Washington Cabernet or Merlot pairs with beef or lamb.

visuals.title: of Washington's vines
visuals.text: grow in the Columbia Valley, east of the Cascades, designated in 1984.

rows.meta: The big one · shared with Oregon

sections.name: New York · Finger Lakes

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Continental. Lakes and rivers soften it inland; the Atlantic softens it on the coast. Growers fight deep winter freezes and summer mold.

lines.label: The lakes
lines.text: The Finger Lakes are 11 glacial lakes, some of the deepest freshwater lakes in the U.S.

know: The Finger Lakes is best known for Riesling.
Dr. Konstantin Frank planted the first vinifera vines in the modern Eastern U.S. in 1957.
Finger Lakes AVA dates from 1982.
Hybrids (Seyval Blanc, Aurore) and native Concord also grow in New York.
Long Island, Hudson River and Lake Erie are other New York AVAs.

items.name: Vitis vinifera

items.name: Hybrids

items.text: A native North American species: Concord.

visuals.title: Vinifera comes east
visuals.text: Dr. Konstantin Frank planted the first vinifera vines in the modern Eastern U.S., then opened Vinifera Wine Cellars in 1962.

sections.name: Canada

lines.label: Where
lines.text: Wine is made in at least nine provinces, mostly British Columbia and Ontario. The deep Great Lakes rarely freeze and soften the winters.

lines.label: The law
lines.text: Canada has no national wine law; each province sets its own. VQA (Vintners Quality Alliance) regulates premium wine.

know: Canada is a leading Icewine producer, and Ontario makes 90% of it.
Icewine grapes freeze naturally on the vine and are picked below -8 °C.
Icewine grapes: Riesling, Cabernet Franc and Vidal.
Every VQA Ontario wine is 100% Ontario grapes.
Main areas: Niagara Peninsula (Ontario) and Okanagan Valley (British Columbia).

items.name: Wait
items.text: Grapes stay on the vine and freeze naturally

visuals.title: of Canadian Icewine is from Ontario
visuals.text: The Court calls Canada a leading global Icewine producer.

mixups.why: Willamette (Oregon) is cool and maritime, for Pinot Noir. Columbia Valley (Washington) is warm desert, for Cabernet and Merlot.
Estate Bottled is a legal term with strict rules. Reserve has no legal meaning in the U.S.
75% is the minimum for the grape name; 85% is the minimum from the named AVA.
Both Central Coast. Paso Robles is warm continental; Santa Barbara is cool maritime with fog.

sources: Built from the Court of Master Sommeliers Americas Introductory Course Guide and Curriculum Guide, TTB rules in 27 CFR part 4 (eCFR), Napa Valley Vintners, Wine Institute, Oregon Wine Board, Washington State Wine Commission, New York Wine & Grape Foundation, VQA Ontario, and Wine Folly as a secondary source. Checked Oct 31, 2026.

facts.fact: Course Guide Section 8, North America, lists: United States: California, Oregon, Washington, New York State.
The Course Guide names important historical figures as exam content, giving as examples Agoston Haraszthy, Robert Mondavi, André Tchelistcheff, David Lett and Dr. Konstantin Frank.
The Curriculum Guide's Introductory column for Canada: know the general location, climate and style of wine produced in Canada.
27 CFR 4.23(b): a single grape variety may be the type designation if not less than 75 percent of the wine is from that variety, all of it grown in the labeled appellation area.
27 CFR 4.23(a): grape variety names may be used only if the wine is also labeled with an appellation of origin.
27 CFR 4.23(c): wine from a Vitis labrusca variety (such as Concord-type native grapes) may carry the variety name at not less than 51 percent of that variety.
27 CFR 4.25(a): an American appellation of origin is the United States, a State, two or three contiguous States, a county, two or three counties in the same State, or a viticultural area.
27 CFR 4.25(b): a country, State or county appellation needs at least 75 percent of the wine from the named area.
27 CFR 4.25(e)(3): a wine may carry a viticultural area appellation if not less than 85 percent of the wine is from grapes grown inside the viticultural area.
27 CFR 4.25(e)(1): an American viticultural area is a delimited grape-growing region with distinguishing features and a name and boundary set in part 9 of the regulations.
TTB: the names and boundary descriptions of all established AVAs are in TTB regulations, 27 CFR part 9.
TTB: an American Viticultural Area, or AVA, is a specific type of appellation of origin used on wine labels; it lets vintners describe the origin of their wines more accurately.
27 CFR 4.27(a)(1): a vintage-dated wine with a viticultural area appellation needs at least 95 percent of the wine from grapes harvested in the labeled year.
27 CFR 4.27(a)(2): with any other appellation (such as a State or county), at least 85 percent must be from the labeled year.
27 CFR 4.27(a): a vintage wine must be labeled with an appellation of origin.
27 CFR 4.39(m): a vineyard, orchard, farm or ranch name may not be used unless 95 percent of the wine came from that named vineyard.

27 CFR 4.26: 'Estate bottled' needs a viticultural area appellation; the winery must be in that area, grow all the grapes on land it owns or controls there, and crush, ferment, finish, age and bottle the wine in a continuous process on its premises.
Court Curriculum Guide (California, Introductory column): 75% minimum grape variety, 85% minimum for AVA, 95% minimum for vintage, 95% minimum for single vineyard.
Court Curriculum Guide (California): 'Reserve' has no legal meaning.
Court Curriculum Guide (California) label terms: Estate Bottled, Meritage (trademark only), Claret.
Court Curriculum Guide (California): style point - American vs. French oak flavor differences.
Court: the North Coast is the coastal counties north of the San Pablo Bay; climate moderate to warm depending on proximity to the Pacific Ocean or San Pablo Bay.

Court (Introductory): Lake County; Mendocino County: Anderson Valley AVA; Sonoma County: Carneros, Sonoma Coast, Alexander Valley, Russian River Valley, Dry Creek Valley AVAs; Napa County: Carneros, Stags Leap District, Oakville, Rutherford, Howell Mountain AVAs. Match AVAs to counties.
Court physical features: Sonoma Mountain Range, Mayacamas Mountain Range, San Pablo Bay, Vaca Mountain Range, Napa River, Petaluma Wind Gap. Soils: very diverse.
Court winemaking: often extensive use of new French and sometimes American oak for red and white wines; malolactic fermentation often used for white wines, especially Chardonnay.
Court: sparkling wines are produced in cooler areas such as Carneros and Anderson Valley.
Court grapes (North and Central Coast): whites Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc; reds Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Syrah.
Court (Certified column): north Napa is warmer; mountain areas have lower yields and bigger day-night temperature swings.
Court producers (Introductory): Opus One, Robert Mondavi, Beringer.
Court history (California): Agoston Haraszthy, Robert Mondavi, André Tchelistcheff.
Court service: young Cabernet Sauvignon often benefits from decanting; old Cabernet Sauvignon needs decanting for sediment.
Court pairing: match full-bodied wines with food richness and intensity.
Napa Valley Vintners: Napa Valley is just 30 miles long and a few miles wide, and is only 4% of California's wine grape harvest.
Napa Valley Vintners: Napa Valley was the first American Viticultural Area designated in California, in 1981.
Napa Valley Vintners: Napa has a dry Mediterranean climate, which only 2% of the world enjoys.
Napa Valley Vintners: Napa created the first Agricultural Preserve in America, in 1968.
Napa Valley Vintners lists Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Zinfandel and Cabernet Franc among its wines.

Napa Valley Vintners: Los Carneros spans parts of Sonoma and Napa counties above the San Pablo Bay; it is cool, with marine winds off the bay; main grapes Chardonnay, Merlot and Pinot Noir; several sparkling houses are based there.

Napa Valley Vintners: Cabernet Sauvignon dominates Rutherford, at the widest part of the valley with the most sun of the valley-floor AVAs; its benchland gives grainy tannins some call 'Rutherford Dust'.
Napa Valley Vintners: Howell Mountain sits at 1,400 to 2,600 ft on the valley's northeast side, above the fog line, on shallow volcanic soils; Cabernet Sauvignon is a principal grape.
Wine Folly (secondary): Russian River Valley is famous for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
Wine Folly (secondary): Dry Creek Valley is known for Zinfandel and Cabernet Sauvignon.
Wine Folly (secondary): Alexander Valley is known for Cabernet, richly flavored Chardonnay and hillside Merlot.
Wine Folly (secondary): Sonoma Coast is Sonoma County's largest AVA, running along the coast, known for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
Wine Folly (secondary): Carneros spans Napa and Sonoma and is famous for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine.
Court: the Central Coast is the coastal counties south of San Francisco Bay and north of the city of Santa Barbara: Monterey County, San Luis Obispo (Paso Robles AVA) and Santa Barbara County.
Court: Monterey and Santa Barbara are generally cool maritime, cooler closer to the coast; Paso Robles is warm continental with large day-night swings.

Court: Monterey has a northwest-to-southeast mountain range creating a cool wind tunnel; Paso Robles is blocked by mountains to the west with only a small gap; Santa Barbara has an east-to-west range creating a cool wind tunnel and fog.

Court (Certified column): Santa Lucia Highlands (Monterey) and Sta. Rita Hills, Santa Maria Valley, Santa Ynez Valley (Santa Barbara) are cool Pinot Noir and Chardonnay areas; Paso Robles and Happy Canyon are warm.
Wine Institute: California produces an average of 81 percent of total U.S. wine production.
Court: identify the Willamette Valley in relation to Portland, Oregon, and the Columbia Valley in relation to Seattle, Washington, on a map.
Court (Introductory) AVAs: Oregon - Willamette Valley; Washington - Columbia Valley, Yakima Valley, Walla Walla Valley.
Court: Willamette Valley is cool Mediterranean with maritime influence; the Coast Range to the west creates a rain shadow, the Cascades lie to the east.
Court: Willamette Valley grapes - Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris (most widely planted red and white), Chardonnay, Riesling.
Court: Oregon requires 90% minimum for the stated variety (except Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and others) and 95% minimum for the AVA.
Court style: Oregon - dry whites, dry reds, sparkling wines; Washington - dry white and dry red wines.
Court history: David Lett of Eyrie Vineyards.
Court (Certified column) pairings: Willamette Valley Pinot Noir with salmon or butternut squash; Washington Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot with beef or lamb.
Oregon Wine Board: for an Oregon appellation, 100% of the grapes must be from Oregon and 95% from that appellation; 90% or more must be the named variety.
Oregon Wine Board: 18 grape varieties are exempt from the 90% rule and may be blended with up to 25% other varieties.
Oregon Wine Board: Willamette Valley is Oregon's oldest wine region, with two-thirds of the state's wineries and vineyards and more than 700 wineries.
Oregon Wine Board: Willamette Valley soils are marine sedimentary, volcanic and loess; main grapes Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Riesling.
Oregon Wine Board lists eleven nested AVAs in the Willamette Valley, including Dundee Hills, Eola-Amity Hills, Chehalem Mountains, Ribbon Ridge, McMinnville, Yamhill-Carlton and Van Duzer Corridor.
Oregon Wine Board: in 1965 David Lett rooted Pinot Noir cuttings near Corvallis, the first plantings in the Willamette Valley; the vines went to The Eyrie Vineyards in the Dundee Hills.
Oregon Wine Board: in 1979 The Eyrie Vineyards 1975 South Block Reserve Pinot Noir placed in the top 10 at the Gault-Millau Wine Olympiad in Paris.
Oregon Wine Board: in 1988 Burgundy-born Véronique Drouhin made her first vintage for Domaine Drouhin Oregon, putting an international spotlight on Oregon.
Oregon Wine Board: Pinot Noir is 59% of Oregon's planted acres, Pinot Gris 14%, Chardonnay 7%.
Court: Columbia Valley is warm desert; the Cascade Range to the west creates a rain shadow; irrigation is needed.
Court: Columbia Valley grapes - Chardonnay, Riesling, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah.
Court (Certified column): Columbia Valley, Walla Walla Valley and Columbia Gorge are AVAs shared by Washington and Oregon; Washington also has Yakima Valley, Horse Heaven Hills and Red Mountain.
Court (Certified column) history: Missoula Floods; phylloxera is absent in the Columbia Valley because of desert conditions.
Washington State Wine Commission: Columbia Valley was designated in 1984; over 99% of Washington's acreage is planted there; it lies in the rain shadow of the Cascades with 6-8 inches of rain a year.
Washington State Wine Commission: Columbia Valley soils are loess over gravel and slackwater sediment on basalt, shaped by the Missoula Floods over 15,000 years ago.
Washington State Wine Commission: Columbia Valley top varieties are Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, Riesling and Syrah.
Washington State Wine Commission press kit: Washington is the 2nd largest wine producer in the United States, with about 1,000 licensed wineries and 21 AVAs.
Washington State Wine Commission press kit: the growing season sees up to 17 hours of sunlight a day; warm days and cool nights keep natural acidity.
Court: New York State climate is continental, moderated by lakes and rivers inland and the Atlantic Ocean on the coast; Finger Lakes have deep glacial lakes.
Court: New York growers must protect vines from deep freezes in harsh winters and from mold in summer.
Court: New York grapes - Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Chardonnay; Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc. Certified column adds hybrids Aurore and Seyval Blanc and Vitis labrusca Concord.
Court: Introductory AVA is the Finger Lakes; the Certified column adds Hudson River, Lake Erie and Long Island.
Court history (New York): Dr. Konstantin Frank.

New York Wine & Grape Foundation: Finger Lakes AVA established September 1, 1982; 11 glacial lakes, some of the deepest freshwater lakes in the United States; known especially for Riesling as one of North America's finest cool-climate regions.
New York Wine & Grape Foundation: the Finger Lakes has 144 wineries and 10,709 acres of vineyard, growing native, hybrid and vinifera grapes.
New York Wine & Grape Foundation: Dr. Konstantin Frank planted the first vinifera vines in the Eastern United States in modern history in 1957, and opened Vinifera Wine Cellars in 1962.
Court: Canada's main wine areas sit within the 30-50° latitude lines; climates range from cool to continental to desert; the deep Great Lakes rarely freeze and moderate winter.
Court: Canada needs winter-hardy varieties able to survive deep freezes; it makes still wine, sparkling wine and ice wine.
Court (Introductory) grapes for Canada: Chardonnay, Riesling; Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc. The Certified column adds Vidal, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer.
Court (Certified column): vines grown in Canada are Vitis vinifera, native North American species (Vitis labrusca, Vitis riparia), and French-American hybrids such as Vidal.
Court: Canada has no national wine law; each province has its own laws. VQA (Vintners Quality Alliance) is the primary regulatory body for premium wine.
Court: wine is made in at least nine provinces, with the largest concentrations in British Columbia and Ontario.

Court: Canada is a leading global ice wine producer; 90% is made in Ontario; grapes must be frozen on the vine and are often picked in the middle of the night; Riesling and Cabernet Franc are used (Vidal too, per the Certified column).
Court: commercial wine in Canada since the mid-1800s; Prohibition 1916-1927; the first winery license in Ontario issued in the 1970s.

Court (Certified column): Okanagan Valley is British Columbia's main area, on the 50-degree line, continental with very hot summers and very cold winters, moderated by Lake Okanagan; Niagara Peninsula is Ontario's main area.
Court (Certified column): sweet and savory pairings with Icewine; producer Inniskillin (printed 'Inniskillen').
VQA Ontario: Icewine is made from grapes frozen naturally on the vine, harvested when the temperature falls below -8 °C, giving juice of at least 35 degrees Brix; Vidal is the flagship Icewine grape.
VQA Ontario: every VQA wine is 100% grown and crafted in Ontario.
VQA Ontario: a 'VQA Niagara Peninsula' wine is at least 85% Niagara grapes; a vintage date needs 85% or more from that year.

VQA Ontario: the Niagara Peninsula is bordered by Lake Ontario to the north; the Niagara Escarpment runs through it, and breezes between the lake and escarpment moderate temperatures; Riesling, Chardonnay, Gamay Noir, Pinot Noir and Cabernet Franc do well.
Wine Folly (secondary): Okanagan Valley's climate is dry, sunny, hot with a short season, moderated by lakes; best wines are dry reds and whites.

unverified: The Court lists 'Estate Bottled: 100%, must be in the same county' (Certified column). The eCFR text (27 CFR 4.26) instead requires a viticultural area appellation with all grapes grown by the winery in that area; no 'same county' wording was found. The chapter uses the eCFR wording.
The Court gives a single '95% minimum for vintage'. eCFR 27 CFR 4.27 says 95% only with an AVA and 85% with other appellations; the chapter uses the eCFR split.
Napa Valley's number of nested AVAs was not stated on the Napa Valley Vintners page fetched (it links to 17 AVA pages), so no count is given.
Willamette Valley AVA year: the Oregon Wine Board page says 'Established: 1983'; a non-official search snippet said 1984. Not used in cards.

No bios were fetched for Agoston Haraszthy, Robert Mondavi or André Tchelistcheff; they appear only as names the Court lists. Stags Leap District and Oakville have no fetched details beyond their county.
Sonoma AVA grape notes (Russian River, Dry Creek, Alexander Valley, Sonoma Coast) come from Wine Folly (secondary); the Sonoma County Vintners site was not fetched.

Okanagan Valley details come from the Court's Certified column and Wine Folly only; no British Columbia Wine Authority page was fetched. Canada is in the Court Curriculum Guide (Introductory column) but not in the Course Guide's Section 8 list, which names only U.S. states.
Oregon's 18 exempt varieties are not listed by name here; the Court names Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot as examples.
The Court Curriculum Guide is dated 8.2023; figures from trade bodies (Oregon 59% Pinot Noir, Washington 21 AVAs, California 81%) may change year to year.

read.where: Napa Valley is just **30 miles long** and a few miles wide, and makes only **4%** of California’s grape harvest. It has a **dry Mediterranean** climate. It sits in the **North Coast**, which runs moderate to warm depending on how close it is to the Pacific or **San Pablo Bay**.

stops.name: Carneros
stops.text: Shared with **Sonoma**, above **San Pablo Bay**, cooled by marine winds. Main grapes are **Chardonnay**, **Merlot** and **Pinot Noir**, and several sparkling houses are based there.

stops.name: Rutherford
stops.text: The widest, sunniest part of the valley floor. **Cabernet Sauvignon** leads here, with grainy tannins some call **“Rutherford Dust.”**

stops.name: Howell Mountain
stops.text: At **1,400 to 2,600 feet**, above the fog line, on shallow **volcanic** soils. Cabernet Sauvignon is a main grape.

stops.name: Stags Leap District and Oakville
stops.text: Two more Napa County AVAs the Court lists. Know them by county.

stops.name: In the cellar
stops.text: Often lots of **new French oak**, sometimes American, for reds and whites. **Chardonnay** often goes through **malolactic fermentation**.

read.visualIntro: Know which county each AVA sits in:
read.mixup: **Carneros** is in both Napa and Sonoma. The other Napa AVAs here are Napa County only.
read.sayIt: A Napa Cabernet, from California’s first AVA.

read.where: **Sonoma**, **Mendocino** and **Lake** counties sit in the **North Coast**, north of **San Pablo Bay**. Features to know are the **Petaluma Wind Gap** and the **Mayacamas** and **Sonoma** mountain ranges. Cooler spots make **sparkling wine**.

read.bigIdea: The Central Coast runs from cool to warm.
read.where: The **Central Coast** is the coastal counties south of **San Francisco Bay** and north of the city of **Santa Barbara**. The counties to know are **Monterey**, **San Luis Obispo** and **Santa Barbara**. Closer to the coast is cooler.

stops.name: Monterey
stops.text: **Cool maritime**. A northwest-to-southeast mountain range makes a cool **wind tunnel**.

stops.name: Paso Robles
stops.text: **Warm continental**, with big day-night swings. Mountains block the sea, with only a small gap.

stops.name: Santa Barbara
stops.text: **Cool maritime**. Its mountains run **east to west**, making a cool wind tunnel that brings **fog**.

read.mixup: **Paso Robles** is warm continental. **Santa Barbara** is cool maritime, with fog.

read.bigIdea: Oregon’s Willamette Valley is Pinot Noir country.
read.where: The **Willamette Valley** has a **cool Mediterranean** climate with maritime influence. The **Coast Range** to the west makes a **rain shadow**, and the **Cascades** lie to the east. Soils are marine sedimentary, volcanic and **loess**.

stops.name: The grapes
stops.text: **Pinot Noir** is 59% of Oregon’s planted acres. **Pinot Gris** is the top white at 14%, then Chardonnay at 7%.

stops.name: The label
stops.text: A grape name needs **90%** of that grape, with 18 exceptions. **95%** must come from the named appellation, and **100%** from Oregon.

stops.name: The pioneer
stops.text: **David Lett** planted the valley’s first Pinot Noir in 1965. The vines went to **The Eyrie Vineyards** in the Dundee Hills.

read.visualIntro: Oregon asks for more than federal law:
read.mixup: **Willamette Valley** (Oregon) is cool and maritime, for Pinot Noir. **Columbia Valley** (Washington) is warm desert, for Cabernet and Merlot.
read.sayIt: Willamette Valley Pinot Noir is a classic with salmon.

read.bigIdea: Washington’s wine grows in desert, east of the Cascades.
read.where: Over **99%** of Washington’s vineyards are in the **Columbia Valley**. The **Cascade Range** to the west makes a **rain shadow**, so it gets only 6-8 inches of rain a year and needs **irrigation**. Soils are **loess** over gravel and sediment on basalt, shaped by the **Missoula Floods**.

stops.name: The grapes
stops.text: **Cabernet Sauvignon**, **Merlot** and **Syrah** for reds. **Chardonnay** and **Riesling** for whites.

stops.name: The AVAs
stops.text: **Columbia Valley**, **Yakima Valley** and **Walla Walla Valley**. Columbia Valley and Walla Walla Valley cross into Oregon.

stops.name: The style
stops.text: **Dry white** and **dry red** wines. Up to 17 hours of sun a day, and cool nights that keep natural acidity.

read.mixup: **Columbia Valley** is Washington’s warm desert. **Willamette Valley** is Oregon’s cool, maritime Pinot Noir country.
read.sayIt: A Washington Cabernet, great with beef or lamb.

read.bigIdea: The Finger Lakes is New York’s Riesling country.
read.where: New York’s climate is **continental**, softened by lakes and rivers inland and by the **Atlantic** on the coast. Growers must protect vines from **deep winter freezes** and from **mold** in summer. The **Finger Lakes** are **11 glacial lakes**, some of the deepest freshwater lakes in the U.S.

stops.name: Finger Lakes
stops.text: Best known for **Riesling**, as one of North America’s finest **cool-climate** regions. Growers here plant native, hybrid and vinifera grapes.

stops.name: Dr. Konstantin Frank
stops.text: He planted the first **vinifera** vines in the modern Eastern U.S. in 1957, then opened Vinifera Wine Cellars in 1962.

stops.name: Other New York AVAs
stops.text: **Long Island**, **Hudson River** and **Lake Erie**.

read.bigIdea: Canada is one of the world’s leading Icewine makers.
read.where: Wine is made in at least **nine provinces**, mostly **British Columbia** and **Ontario**. The deep **Great Lakes** rarely freeze, which softens the winters. Vines must be **winter-hardy** to survive deep freezes.

stops.name: The law
stops.text: Canada has **no national wine law**; each province sets its own. **VQA** (Vintners Quality Alliance) regulates premium wine.

stops.name: Two main areas
stops.text: The **Niagara Peninsula** in Ontario sits between Lake Ontario and the Niagara Escarpment. The **Okanagan Valley** in British Columbia is moderated by Lake Okanagan.

stops.name: Icewine
stops.text: Grapes **freeze naturally on the vine** and are picked below **-8 °C**, often at night. Riesling, Cabernet Franc and **Vidal** are used, and Ontario makes **90%** of it.

read.mixup: **VQA** is Canada’s quality body. An **AVA** is a U.S. place of origin.
read.sayIt: Icewine is made from grapes that froze on the vine. It’s a sweet wine.
